english.html: — namely twelve years and more — absent from his wife, and so for having been the cause of the disorder which has followed from it <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>, as has been copiously demonstrated above <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>; whence follows the common decision of the law, that he who gives the occasion of a misdeed renders himself guilty of the crime <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>. The third and last: that during the time of his absence he withdrew to the enemy, and served them in the business of war against our King his natural prince, falling thereby into the crime of lese-majesty <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>. Nevertheless the Court dismissed him from the case and suit, considering that what he did proceeded from no evil will, but from a heat and lightness of youth which then boiled within him — of which the proper and peculiar vice (says Seneca) is to be unable to govern or tame the fury of the impetuous assaults which the ardour of that inconsiderate age, ever inclined and prone to evil <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup>, incessantly delivers to it <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup>. And as prudence is the proper virtue of old age, so instability also, indiscretion and rashness are peculiar to youth <sup class="mk" data-key="h">h</sup>, covetous of changing country, of seeing new things and of leaving the present and best-loved ones, as Horace learnedly describes when he says <sup class="mk" data-key="i">i</sup>:

notes.citation: Decretum of Gratian, Part II, c. Si tu abstines, cited by Coras at C. 27 q. 2 (locus not verified; at annot-002 {a} he cited the same canon at C. 28 q. 2, and its modern place is probably among Augustine's texts on the conjugal debt in C. 33 q. 5)
notes.original: c. tu abſtines. xxvij. q. ij.
notes.gloss: Augustine, De adulterinis coniugiis: if you abstain without your wife's consent you give her licence to fornicate, and her sin is imputed to your abstinence — quoted in full at annot-002.

notes.citation: Coras, Annotation II (annot-002), on the husband's long absence
Digest 9.2 (Ad legem Aquiliam), l. Qui occidit (D. 9.2.7, Ulpian), the penultimate paragraph (§ 7, unverified); Code 7.17 (De assertione tollenda), l. 1, § fin.
notes.original: l. qui occidit. P. penul. D. ad l. Aquil. l. j. P. fi. C. de aſſat. tollẽ.
notes.gloss: Cited for the maxim that he who gives the occasion of a harm is taken to have done it. The print's aſſat. is aſſert.

notes.citation: Digest 48.4 (Ad legem Iuliam maiestatis), ll. 1, 2 and 4 (the last numeral is uncertain in the print: iiij or iij)
notes.original: l. i. l. ij. l. iiij. D. ad l. Iuli. maieſta.
notes.gloss: D. 48.4.1 (Ulpian) defines the crime, including sending aid to the enemy; D. 48.4.2 extends it to him who gives help to the enemies of the Roman people; ll. 3 and 4 both concern going over to or aiding the enemy, so the print's numeral cannot be settled by the content.

notes.citation: Decretum, C. 12 q. 1, c. 1 (bearing on the point not verified)
Seneca, Troades (the sixth tragedy in the Renaissance order), line 250
notes.original: Seneca en ſa vi tragedie inſcrite, Troas.
notes.gloss: Iuvenile vitium est regere non posse impetum — it is the vice of youth not to be able to govern its impulse; Agamemnon to Pyrrhus. The print's Tioas is a wrong sort for Troas.

notes.citation: Cicero, De senectute (On Old Age); Decretum, C. 12 q. 1, c. 1, as at {f}
notes.original: Ciceron au liure de Senectute. c. i. xij. q. i.
notes.gloss: Cicero, De sen. 20: rashness belongs to youth, prudence to age — temeritas est videlicet florentis aetatis, prudentia senescentis.

Imberbis iuvenis, tandem custode remoto, / gaudet equis canibusque et aprici gramine Campi, / cereus in vitium flecti, monitoribus asper, / utilium tardus provisor, prodigus aeris, / sublimis cupidusque et amata relinquere pernix. The print has Vitilium for utilium and Cæreus for cereus.

english.html: The beardless youth, his guardian at last removed, delights in horses and dogs and the grass of the sunny Campus; wax to be bent to vice, harsh to those who warn him, slow to provide for what is useful, prodigal of money, high-spirited and full of desires, and swift to abandon what he has loved.

And as for saying that the said Martin gave occasion to the said de Rols his wife to receive another for her husband, and so that if there was a fault it is to be imputed to him <sup class="mk" data-key="k">k</sup>: besides that this reason has been sufficiently answered above <sup class="mk" data-key="l">l</sup>, it must be considered that the occasions of doing evil are of two kinds. Troas is Seneca's Troades, the sixth tragedy in the Renaissance order, where the line Coras paraphrases stands (Tro. 250, iuvenile vitium est regere non posse impetum); Tioas is no title.
ead. = eadem (causa et quaestione), the canon Si tu abstines in the same place as at {b}; and. is no abbreviation.
